lesson.text: Quick memory: what should you do after a mistake? (Own up, say sorry and put it right.) Today: kindness and respect.
Respect means treating people well because every person matters. It means listening when they speak, being polite, and caring about their feelings and their things.

People are different in many ways. They look different, speak different languages and eat different food. Families and beliefs differ too. What is easy for one person is hard for another. Everyone deserves respect.
Differences make the world more fun! Families have many special days, like Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Hanukkah and Lunar New Year. Learning about them helps us understand each other.
Kindness is doing or saying something good for someone else: sharing, helping, asking “Do you want to join in?” or saying “Well done!”

panels.say: Do you want to join in?

lesson.text: Before you act, imagine being in the other person's shoes. How would you feel? This is called empathy. It helps you choose kind words.
If someone is unkind to another person, you can help: stay kind yourself, check the person is all right, and tell a grown-up you trust.
Try it in the world: build a welcome garden in your world with a bench and flowers, and invite a friend to add something. Say one kind thing about what they built.

choices: treating people well because they matter
exercises.explain: Respect means treating everyone well: listening, being polite and caring about their feelings.

exercises.prompt: Which is a kind thing to say to someone left out?
exercises.hint: Which words would make you feel welcome?
choices: Do you want to join in?
exercises.explain: Asking them to join in is kind and helps them feel welcome.

exercises.prompt: People who are different from you deserve respect too.
exercises.explain: True: everyone deserves respect, however different they are.

exercises.prompt: Laughing at someone's accent is respectful.
exercises.hint: How would you feel if people laughed at how you speak?
exercises.explain: False: it is unkind. Many people speak more than one language, with different accents.

exercises.hint: Remember being in the other person's shoes.
exercises.explain: Empathy is imagining how someone else feels, which helps us be kind.

exercises.prompt: Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Hanukkah are all…
exercises.hint: Remember the lesson card about differences.
exercises.explain: They are festivals that many families around the world celebrate.

exercises.prompt: You can respect someone even if you like different things.
exercises.hint: Do you need to agree with someone to treat them well?
exercises.explain: True: respect is treating people well, even when you like different things.

exercises.prompt: Mimi's new neighbour speaks a different language. What is a respectful thing to do?
exercises.hint: How could you help someone new feel welcome?
choices: smile, and learn to say hello her way
exercises.explain: Smiling and learning a word in her language shows respect and kindness.

exercises.prompt: Bram sees a friend being teased. What is the best thing to do?
exercises.hint: Stay kind yourself, and get help.
choices: check the friend is all right, tell a grown-up
exercises.explain: Checking the friend is all right and telling a trusted grown-up helps without being unkind.

exercises.prompt: Which shows respect for someone's things?
exercises.hint: How would you like people to treat your things?
exercises.explain: Asking before you borrow shows you respect that the thing belongs to them.

exercises.prompt: Being kind only counts if someone sees you do it.
exercises.hint: Does the person you helped feel better either way?
exercises.explain: False: kindness counts whether or not anyone sees it. Holding a door or picking up a dropped pencil still helps someone, and that is what matters.

exercises.prompt: Zara builds differently from her friend. How can she show respect?
exercises.hint: Different ways can both be good.
choices: say what she likes about her friend's way
say only her way is right
exercises.explain: Saying what she likes about her friend's way shows respect for someone different.

exercises.prompt: Everyone finds the same things easy.
exercises.hint: Is there something you find easy that a friend finds hard, or the other way round?
exercises.explain: False: people find different things easy or hard. Bram reads fast but finds drawing hard; Zara draws well but reads slowly. That is fine, and everyone deserves respect.

exercises.hint: How would each one make the other person feel?
exercises.explain: Kind: asking someone to join in, asking before you borrow. Unkind: laughing at an accent, taking without asking.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
exercises.hint: Look back at the cards: which word is about another person's shoes?
exercises.explain: Respect is treating people well, kindness is doing good for someone, and empathy is imagining how they feel.

items: Do you want to join in?
exercises.hint: How would each one make the other person feel?
exercises.explain: Asking someone to join in and saying well done are kind. Leaving someone out and laughing at a mistake are unkind.

exercises.prompt: Someone is unkind to another child. Put what you do in order.
items: Check the child is all right.
exercises.hint: Start with yourself, then the child who was hurt.
exercises.explain: Stay kind yourself, check the child is all right, then tell a grown-up you trust.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: respect for the person, or respect for their things?
items: asking before you borrow her pen
learning her way of saying hello
exercises.hint: Is it about how you treat someone, or how you treat what belongs to them?
exercises.explain: The person: listening, learning her hello and waiting your turn. Their things: asking before you borrow, putting the book back and not drawing on her picture.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to a kind, respectful answer.
items: you want to borrow a pen
matches: check on them, tell a grown-up
say what you like about it
exercises.hint: Imagine being in each person's shoes. What would help them?
exercises.explain: A different build: say what you like about it. A child alone: ask them to join in. Someone teased: check on them and tell a grown-up. A pen: ask first.
